Classification with Decision Trees and k-Nearest Neighbors — MASS::biopsy

Aminur Refat Faisal

2026-08-20

1. Overview

This notebook re-runs the complete supervised classification pipeline from the iris version of this notebook, but this time on R’s built-in MASS::biopsy dataset — a binary, medical-diagnosis classification problem (benign vs. malignant breast tumors) with 9 numeric, fairly correlated features instead of iris’s 4. The goal is to see how a Decision Tree and k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) behave when: (a) there are only two classes instead of three, (b) the features are more numerous and more correlated with each other, and (c) the raw data actually contains missing values that must be handled before modeling.

The pipeline still has 9 stages:

  1. Load & explore data — inspect structure, summary statistics, missing values, and class balance.
  2. Visualize relationships — pairwise scatterplots, boxplots by class, and a correlation heatmap.
  3. Preprocess — drop the ID column, handle missing values, and split into train/test sets.
  4. Decision Tree — model building — fit a classification tree with rpart.
  5. Decision Tree — visualization & pruning — plot the tree and control overfitting via the complexity parameter.
  6. Decision Tree — evaluation — confusion matrix, accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, variable importance.
  7. KNN — preprocessing & model building — scale features (required for KNN) and fit models across a range of k.
  8. KNN — evaluation — confusion matrix, accuracy, and an accuracy-vs-k curve to select the best k.
  9. Model comparison, ROC/AUC, and save outputs — compare both models side by side and export results.

Why this matters: With iris, both algorithms achieved near-perfect accuracy because the petal measurements separated the three species almost perfectly. biopsy is a tougher, more realistic test: 9 correlated features, a real (if small) amount of missing data, and — because this is a medical-diagnosis task — the cost of errors is asymmetric. Missing a malignant tumor (a false negative) is far more dangerous than flagging a benign one for a second look (a false positive), so beyond plain accuracy we also look at sensitivity for the malignant class below.

2. Packages

# List of required packages
packages <- c("tidyverse", "caret", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
              "class", "GGally", "e1071", "MASS", "pROC")

# Check which packages are already installed on this machine
installed_packages <- rownames(installed.packages())

for (pkg in packages) {
  # Install only if missing
  if (!(pkg %in% installed_packages)) {
    install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
  }
  # Load the package into the current session
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

# NOTE: MASS::select() and dplyr::select() clash. We load MASS only for its
# `biopsy` dataset and always call dplyr's version explicitly as
# dplyr::select() further down, to avoid silently masking tidyverse verbs.

# Fix the random seed everywhere in this notebook so that the train/test
# split, tree fitting (which has some randomness in tie-breaking), and KNN
# results are exactly reproducible on re-run.
set.seed(42)

3. The Dataset: MASS::biopsy

biopsy is one of R’s built-in datasets (no download needed — just type data(biopsy)). It contains 699 fine-needle-aspirate biopsy samples from the Wisconsin Breast Cancer study, each described by 9 cytological characteristics scored on a 1–10 scale, with a binary outcome: whether the tumor was ultimately diagnosed as benign or malignant. Unlike iris, this dataset has (a) only two classes, (b) noticeably correlated features (several attributes co-vary with how abnormal a cell looks overall), and (c) a small amount of real missing data — a good stress test for a pipeline built on clean data.

data(biopsy)

# ---- Basic structure ----
str(biopsy)

Variables:

Column Type Description
ID character Sample code number — identifier only, not a predictive feature
V1 numeric (1–10) Clump Thickness
V2 numeric (1–10) Uniformity of Cell Size
V3 numeric (1–10) Uniformity of Cell Shape
V4 numeric (1–10) Marginal Adhesion
V5 numeric (1–10) Single Epithelial Cell Size
V6 numeric (1–10) Bare Nuclei (contains missing values)
V7 numeric (1–10) Bland Chromatin
V8 numeric (1–10) Normal Nucleoli
V9 numeric (1–10) Mitoses
class factor (2 levels) Target variable — benign / malignant 
# Always check for missing values before modeling — neither rpart nor knn()
# handles NAs gracefully by default. Unlike iris, biopsy actually has some.
cat("Total missing values:", sum(is.na(biopsy)), "\n")
## Total missing values: 16
colSums(is.na(biopsy))
##    ID    V1    V2    V3    V4    V5    V6    V7    V8    V9 class 
##     0     0     0     0     0     0    16     0     0     0     0

V6 (Bare Nuclei) has missing values. We drop the ID column (it carries no predictive information) and drop rows with missing V6, since it’s a small fraction of the data and neither rpart nor knn() can use rows with NAs in a predictor out of the box.

biopsy_clean <- biopsy %>%
  dplyr::select(-ID) %>%
  drop_na()

cat("Rows before cleaning:", nrow(biopsy), "\n")
## Rows before cleaning: 699
cat("Rows after cleaning: ", nrow(biopsy_clean), "\n")
## Rows after cleaning:  683
cat("\nClass balance after cleaning:\n")
## 
## Class balance after cleaning:
print(table(biopsy_clean$class))
## 
##    benign malignant 
##       444       239

4. Exploratory Visualization

Before modeling, it helps to see how separable the classes are and how correlated the features are with each other.

# ggpairs() draws every pairwise combination of the 9 numeric features,
# colored by class, plus per-feature density plots on the diagonal.
# With 9 features this grid is larger (and slower to render) than iris's —
# that density is itself the point: these features are far more numerous
# and correlated than iris's 4.
GGally::ggpairs(
  biopsy_clean,
  columns = 1:9,
  aes(color = class, alpha = 0.6)
) +
  theme_minimal()

# Reshape to long format so all 9 features can be faceted in one ggplot call
biopsy_long <- biopsy_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -class, names_to = "Feature", values_to = "Value")

ggplot(biopsy_long, aes(x = class, y = Value, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ Feature, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Each Feature by Diagnosis",
       x = NULL, y = "Score (1-10)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# A correlation heatmap makes the "many correlated numeric features" aspect
# of this dataset explicit, which iris's 4 loosely-related measurements
# didn't really show.
cor_matrix <- biopsy_clean %>%
  dplyr::select(-class) %>%
  cor()

cor_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))

ggplot(cor_df, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Freq, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick",
                        midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Corr.") +
  labs(title = "Feature Correlation Matrix", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

What to notice: every single feature separates benign from malignant to some degree (malignant samples score higher on essentially all 9 characteristics), which is different from iris, where two features (sepal measurements) were nearly useless. But the correlation heatmap also shows that many of these features are strongly correlated with one another (e.g., V2/V3, cell size and shape uniformity) — redundant information that a tree can exploit for a compact model, but that adds noise-free “extra” dimensions for KNN’s distance calculation.

5. Preprocessing: Train/Test Split

We hold out part of the data to evaluate generalization — i.e., how well the model performs on biopsies it has never seen, not just the ones it was fit on.

# createDataPartition() performs STRATIFIED sampling: it preserves the
# original class proportions in both the train and test sets, which matters
# here since biopsy's classes are imbalanced (~65% benign / ~35% malignant)
# and a naive random split could distort that further by chance.
train_index <- createDataPartition(biopsy_clean$class, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)

train_data <- biopsy_clean[train_index, ]
test_data  <- biopsy_clean[-train_index, ]

cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
## Training rows: 479
cat("Testing rows: ", nrow(test_data), "\n")
## Testing rows:  204
# Confirm the class balance was preserved in both sets
cat("\nTraining set class balance:\n")
## 
## Training set class balance:
print(table(train_data$class))
## 
##    benign malignant 
##       311       168
cat("\nTest set class balance:\n")
## 
## Test set class balance:
print(table(test_data$class))
## 
##    benign malignant 
##       133        71

Note on scaling: as with iris, decision trees split on one feature at a time using threshold rules, so feature scale doesn’t affect the tree’s structure — no scaling is needed for Section 6. KNN still needs scaling for Section 8, even though every biopsy feature already lives on the same 1–10 scale — features with more spread would otherwise still dominate the Euclidean distance.

6. Decision Tree — Model Building

# method = "class" tells rpart this is a classification (not regression) tree.
tree_model <- rpart(
  class ~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V8 + V9,
  data = train_data,
  method = "class"
)

# A text summary of the fitted tree: each node shows the split rule,
# number of observations, misclassifications, and predicted class.
print(tree_model)
## n= 479 
## 
## node), split, n, loss, yval, (yprob)
##       * denotes terminal node
## 
## 1) root 479 168 benign (0.64926931 0.35073069)  
##   2) V2< 2.5 293   9 benign (0.96928328 0.03071672) *
##   3) V2>=2.5 186  27 malignant (0.14516129 0.85483871)  
##     6) V3< 2.5 15   2 benign (0.86666667 0.13333333) *
##     7) V3>=2.5 171  14 malignant (0.08187135 0.91812865) *

6.1 Visualizing the Tree

rpart.plot(
  tree_model,
  type = 3, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  main = "Classification Tree for Breast Biopsy Diagnosis",
  box.palette = "auto"
)

6.2 Variable Importance

# Higher = more influential in the tree's decisions. Because several
# features are correlated (Section 4), expect the top few to dominate while
# some correlated "duplicates" score lower — the tree only needs one of a
# correlated pair to make an equally good split.
tree_model$variable.importance
##       V2       V3       V5       V8       V6       V7 
## 154.5461 139.9592 113.0014 110.5088 106.3543 104.2370

7. Decision Tree — Pruning

printcp(tree_model)
## 
## Classification tree:
## rpart(formula = class ~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V8 + 
##     V9, data = train_data, method = "class")
## 
## Variables actually used in tree construction:
## [1] V2 V3
## 
## Root node error: 168/479 = 0.35073
## 
## n= 479 
## 
##         CP nsplit rel error  xerror     xstd
## 1 0.785714      0   1.00000 1.00000 0.062167
## 2 0.065476      1   0.21429 0.27976 0.038754
## 3 0.010000      2   0.14881 0.17262 0.031069
plotcp(tree_model)  # visualizes error vs. tree size; look for the "elbow"

# Standard rule of thumb: pick the cp with the lowest cross-validated
# error (xerror). which.min() finds that row automatically so this
# generalizes to any dataset without hand-reading the table above.
best_cp <- tree_model$cptable[which.min(tree_model$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
cat("Selected cp for pruning:", best_cp, "\n")
## Selected cp for pruning: 0.01
pruned_tree <- prune(tree_model, cp = best_cp)

rpart.plot(
  pruned_tree,
  type = 3, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  main = "Pruned Classification Tree",
  box.palette = "auto"
)

On this dataset: with 9 correlated features and ~480 training rows, biopsy gives the pruning step more to actually do than iris did — watch plotcp() for whether the cross-validated error keeps dropping past the first split or plateaus early.

7.1 Predictions and Evaluation

tree_preds <- predict(pruned_tree, newdata = test_data, type = "class")

# positive = "malignant": in a medical-diagnosis setting we care most about
# correctly flagging the malignant (positive) cases, so we tell caret which
# level to treat as "positive" for Sensitivity/Specificity, rather than
# letting it default to the alphabetically-first level ("benign").
tree_cm <- confusionMatrix(tree_preds, test_data$class, positive = "malignant")
tree_cm
## Confusion Matrix and Statistics
## 
##            Reference
## Prediction  benign malignant
##   benign       127         6
##   malignant      6        65
##                                           
##                Accuracy : 0.9412          
##                  95% CI : (0.8995, 0.9692)
##     No Information Rate : 0.652           
##     P-Value [Acc > NIR] : <2e-16          
##                                           
##                   Kappa : 0.8704          
##                                           
##  Mcnemar's Test P-Value : 1               
##                                           
##             Sensitivity : 0.9155          
##             Specificity : 0.9549          
##          Pos Pred Value : 0.9155          
##          Neg Pred Value : 0.9549          
##              Prevalence : 0.3480          
##          Detection Rate : 0.3186          
##    Detection Prevalence : 0.3480          
##       Balanced Accuracy : 0.9352          
##                                           
##        'Positive' Class : malignant       
## 
as.data.frame(tree_cm$table) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Decision Tree — Confusion Matrix", x = "Actual", y = "Predicted") +
  theme_minimal()

8. k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

8.1 Feature Scaling

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# IMPORTANT: we compute the scaling parameters (mean, sd) from the
# TRAINING set only, then apply that SAME transformation to the test set,
# to avoid leaking test-set information into training.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
feature_cols <- c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4", "V5", "V6", "V7", "V8", "V9")

preproc <- preProcess(train_data[, feature_cols], method = c("center", "scale"))

train_scaled <- predict(preproc, train_data[, feature_cols])
test_scaled  <- predict(preproc, test_data[, feature_cols])

# Labels are kept separately, since knn() takes them as their own argument
train_labels <- train_data$class
test_labels  <- test_data$class

summary(train_scaled)  # each feature should now have mean ~0, sd ~1

8.2 Choosing k

k_values <- 1:20

# For each candidate k, fit and evaluate a KNN model, storing accuracy
accuracy_by_k <- map_dbl(k_values, function(k) {
  pred <- knn(train = train_scaled, test = test_scaled,
              cl = train_labels, k = k)
  mean(pred == test_labels)
})

k_results <- tibble(k = k_values, accuracy = accuracy_by_k)
best_k <- k_results$k[which.max(k_results$accuracy)]

cat("Best k (by test accuracy):", best_k, "\n")
## Best k (by test accuracy): 3
ggplot(k_results, aes(x = k, y = accuracy)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_k, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_values) +
  labs(title = "KNN Accuracy vs. k",
       subtitle = paste("Best k =", best_k),
       x = "k (number of neighbors)", y = "Test Accuracy") +
  theme_minimal()

Same methodological caveat as before: selecting k by directly maximizing test-set accuracy risks mild overfitting to the test set. Section 8.4 repeats the more rigorous cross-validated approach.

8.3 Final KNN Model and Evaluation

knn_preds <- knn(train = train_scaled, test = test_scaled,
                  cl = train_labels, k = best_k)

knn_cm <- confusionMatrix(knn_preds, test_labels, positive = "malignant")
knn_cm

  labs(title = paste0("KNN (k=", best_k, ") — Confusion Matrix"),
       x = "Actual", y = "Predicted") +
  theme_minimal()

8.4 (Recommended) Cross-Validated KNN via caret

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, classProbs = TRUE)

knn_cv_model <- train(
  class ~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 + V6 + V7 + V8 + V9,
  data = train_data,
  method = "knn",
  trControl = ctrl,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),   # scaling is applied inside each CV fold
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = 1:20)
)

knn_cv_model

# Evaluate the cross-validation-selected model once, on the held-out test set
knn_cv_preds <- predict(knn_cv_model, newdata = test_data)
knn_cv_cm <- confusionMatrix(knn_cv_preds, test_data$class, positive = "malignant")

9. Model Comparison

comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Decision Tree (pruned)", "KNN (test-tuned)", "KNN (cross-validated)"),
  Accuracy = c(
    tree_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    knn_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    knn_cv_cm$overall["Accuracy"]
  ),
  Kappa = c(
    tree_cm$overall["Kappa"],
    knn_cm$overall["Kappa"],
    knn_cv_cm$overall["Kappa"]
  ),
  # Sensitivity for the "malignant" class matters most clinically here:
  # a false negative (calling a malignant tumor benign) is the costly error.
  Sensitivity_Malignant = c(
    tree_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    knn_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    knn_cv_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  ),
  Specificity_Benign = c(
    tree_cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    knn_cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    knn_cv_cm$byClass["Specificity"]
  )
)

comparison
## # A tibble: 3 × 5
##   Model                  Accuracy Kappa Sensitivity_Malignant Specificity_Benign
##   <chr>                     <dbl> <dbl>                 <dbl>              <dbl>
## 1 Decision Tree (pruned)    0.941 0.870                 0.915              0.955
## 2 KNN (test-tuned)          0.985 0.967                 0.958              1    
## 3 KNN (cross-validated)     0.985 0.967                 0.972              0.992
Aspect Decision Tree KNN
How it decides Learns explicit if–then split rules Majority vote among k nearest points
Feature scaling required? No Yes — critical
Interpretability High — the tree itself is the explanation Low — no explicit model to inspect
Handles correlated features Naturally — picks one, ignores redundant ones Uses all of them in every distance calculation
Sensitive to Overfitting if unpruned Choice of k; irrelevant/unscaled features; class imbalance
Decision boundary shape Axis-aligned rectangles Arbitrarily shaped, locally adaptive

On biopsy vs. iris: both models still perform well here (breast biopsy features are strongly diagnostic), but accuracy alone hides more than it did with iris’s 3 well-separated classes. Because the classes are imbalanced (~65/35) and errors are asymmetric, the sensitivity for the malignant class in the table above is the number worth scrutinizing most — a model with high overall accuracy but lower malignant-class sensitivity is quietly missing real cancers.

9.1 Bonus: ROC / AUC

Because biopsy is binary (unlike iris’s 3 classes), ROC/AUC analysis is directly applicable without a one-vs-rest workaround — this was flagged as a “next step” in the iris version, and it’s straightforward to add here.

# Class probabilities (not just hard class labels) are needed for ROC curves
tree_probs   <- predict(pruned_tree, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[, "malignant"]
knn_cv_probs <- predict(knn_cv_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[, "malignant"]

roc_tree <- roc(test_data$class, tree_probs, levels = c("benign", "malignant"))
roc_knn  <- roc(test_data$class, knn_cv_probs, levels = c("benign", "malignant"))

cat("Decision Tree AUC:", round(auc(roc_tree), 3), "\n")
## Decision Tree AUC: 0.954
cat("KNN (cross-validated) AUC:", round(auc(roc_knn), 3), "\n")
## KNN (cross-validated) AUC: 0.992
plot(roc_tree, col = "steelblue", main = "ROC Curves: Decision Tree vs. KNN")
plot(roc_knn, col = "darkorange", add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Decision Tree", "KNN (CV)"),
       col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"), lwd = 2)

write_csv(

write_csv(comparison, "biopsy_model_comparison.csv")

11. Summary

In this notebook, re-ran the classification pipeline MASS::biopsy, and learned how it behaves differently when:

  • The problem is binary rather than 3-class (letting us use Sensitivity/Specificity and ROC/AUC directly, without a one-vs-rest workaround).
  • The dataset has real missing values that must be explicitly handled before modeling (drop_na()), unlike iris’s clean data.
  • There are 9 correlated features instead of 4 loosely-related ones — visible in the correlation heatmap in Section 4 — which the tree handles by simply picking one of each redundant pair, while KNN’s distance calculation uses all 9 regardless.
  • Class imbalance (~65% benign / ~35% malignant) makes plain accuracy less informative than the per-class Sensitivity/Specificity breakdown.

Next steps to try on your own:

  • Re-run this notebook on another built-in dataset, e.g. mlbench::Sonar (binary classification, many correlated numeric features) or MASS::biopsy (medical diagnosis), to see how the two models’ relative performance changes when classes overlap more or features are noisier.
  • Extend Section 9 with ROC/AUC analysis (pROC package) — straightforward for binary classification, requires a one-vs-rest approach for the 3-class case here.
  • Compare both models against a third baseline, such as logistic regression (binary case) or nnet::multinom (multi-class), to place their accuracy in context.
  • Investigate feature selection: refit the Decision Tree and KNN using only Petal.Length and Petal.Width (the two most separating features from Section 4) and see whether accuracy changes.
